questions.problem: What is the limit of the sequence ${a}_{n}=\frac{8{n}^{6}+4{n}^{5}}{8{n}^{4}+10}$ for $n\ge 1?$
questions.worked_solution:
The dominant term in the denominator is $8{n}^{4},$ so we divide the numerator and the denominator by ${n}^{4}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{8{n}^{6}+4{n}^{5}}{8{n}^{4}+10} & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{8{n}^{6}}{{n}^{4}}+\frac{4{n}^{5}}{{n}^{4}})}{(\frac{8{n}^{4}}{{n}^{4}}+\frac{10}{{n}^{4}})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{8{n}^{2}+4n}{(8+\frac{10}{{n}^{4}})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{8{n}^{2}+4n}{8+0} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }({n}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}n) \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

The limit does not exist, so the sequence diverges.

questions.problem:
Which of the following sequences diverge?

- ${a}_{n}=\frac{{n}^{5}}{2{n}^{5}-1}$ for $n\ge 1$
- ${a}_{n}=\frac{n-{n}^{5}}{2-{n}^{4}}$ for $n\ge 1$
- ${a}_{n}=\frac{5}{{n}^{6}}$ for $n\ge 1$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's analyze each sequence in turn. We need to calculate the limit of each sequence as $n$ approaches infinity.

- In sequence I,  the dominant term in the denominator is $2{n}^{5},$ so we divide the numerator and the denominator by ${n}^{5}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n} & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{{n}^{5}}{2{n}^{5}-1} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{{n}^{5}}{{n}^{5}})}{(\frac{2{n}^{5}}{{n}^{5}}-\frac{1}{{n}^{5}})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{1}{(2-\frac{1}{{n}^{5}})} \\  & =\frac{1}{2-0} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The limit exists, so the sequence converges.

- In sequence II, the dominant term in the denominator is $-{n}^{4},$ so we divide the numerator and the denominator by ${n}^{4}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n} & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{n-{n}^{5}}{2-{n}^{4}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{n}{{n}^{4}}-\frac{{n}^{5}}{{n}^{4}})}{(\frac{2}{{n}^{4}}-\frac{{n}^{4}}{{n}^{4}})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{1}{{n}^{3}}-n)}{(\frac{2}{{n}^{4}}-1)} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{0-n}{0-1} \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

The limit does not exist, so the sequence diverges.

- In sequence III,  the limit is

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n}={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{5}{{n}^{6}}=0.
$$

The limit exists, so the sequence converges.

In conclusion, sequence II diverges.

questions.problem: What is the limit of the sequence ${a}_{n}=\frac{({n}^{2}+2)({n}^{2}-2)}{{n}^{2}(3-n)}$ for $n>3?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we multiply out the numerator and denominator of the sequence and get

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{({n}^{2}+2)({n}^{2}-2)}{{n}^{2}(3-n)}=\frac{{n}^{4}-4}{3{n}^{2}-{n}^{3}}.
$$

So to find the limit, we will need to compute

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n}={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{{n}^{4}-4}{3{n}^{2}-{n}^{3}}.
$$

The dominant term in the denominator is $-{n}^{3},$ so we divide the numerator and the denominator by ${n}^{3}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{{n}^{4}-4}{3{n}^{2}-{n}^{3}} & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{{n}^{4}}{{n}^{3}}-\frac{4}{{n}^{3}})}{(\frac{3{n}^{2}}{{n}^{3}}-\frac{{n}^{3}}{{n}^{3}})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(n-\frac{4}{{n}^{3}})}{(\frac{3}{n}-1)} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{n-0}{0-1} \\  & =-\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the sequence diverges.

questions.problem: What is the limit of the sequence ${a}_{n}=\frac{({n}^{3}+1)({n}^{3}-1)}{n(2-n)}$ for $n>2?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we multiply out the numerator and denominator of the sequence and get

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{({n}^{3}+1)({n}^{3}-1)}{n(2-n)}=\frac{{n}^{6}-1}{2n-{n}^{2}}.
$$

So to find the limit, we will need to compute

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n}={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{{n}^{6}-1}{2n-{n}^{2}}.
$$

The dominant term in the denominator is $-{n}^{2},$ so we divide the numerator and the denominator by ${n}^{2}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{{n}^{6}-1}{2n-{n}^{2}} & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{{n}^{6}}{{n}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{n}^{2}})}{(\frac{2n}{{n}^{2}}-\frac{{n}^{2}}{{n}^{2}})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{({n}^{4}-\frac{1}{{n}^{2}})}{(\frac{2}{n}-1)} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{{n}^{4}-0}{0-1} \\  & =-\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the sequence diverges.

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Limit of a Factored Rational Sequence
questions.worked_solution:
First, we multiply out the numerator and denominator of the sequence and get

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{(5n-3)(5n+3)}{n(2-25n)}=\frac{25{n}^{2}-9}{2n-25{n}^{2}}.
$$

So to find the limit, we will need to compute

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n}={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{25{n}^{2}-9}{2n-25{n}^{2}}.
$$

The dominant term in the denominator is $-25{n}^{2},$ so we divide the numerator and the denominator by ${n}^{2}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n} & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{25{n}^{2}-9}{2n-25{n}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{25{n}^{2}}{{n}^{2}}-\frac{9}{{n}^{2}})}{(\frac{2n}{{n}^{2}}-\frac{25{n}^{2}}{{n}^{2}})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(25-\frac{9}{{n}^{2}})}{(\frac{2}{n}-25)} \\  & =\frac{25-0}{0-25} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the sequence converges and its limit is $-1.$
